Everyone in the village knew that Helen Turrell, a respectable woman of good family, had always done her duty by everyone, and above all by her only brothers unfortunate child. <break time="0.8s" /> George, who served as a police inspector in India, had become entangled with the daughter of a retired sergeant, and then he was killed by a fall from his horse. <break time="0.8s" /> His death came only a few weeks before his son was born, and Helen, then resting in the south of France for her weak lungs, resolved to take charge of the child. <break time="0.8s" /> Helen arranged for the baby to be brought from Bombay to Marseilles, where she met him and took him into her own care at once. <break time="0.8s" /> Soon the baby fell ill with dysentery because of a careless nurse, whom Helen promptly dismissed before nursing the child back to health herself. <break time="0.8s" /> Late that autumn she came home to Hampshire with the boy, whom she had already had christened Michael, and settled down to raise him in her own house. <break time="0.8s" /> Helen never tried to hide the facts, for she believed that scandals only grow larger when they are hushed up, and so she spoke of them freely to anyone who asked. <break time="0.8s" /> As she told it, Michael was simply her dead brothers son, and she had agreed, out of duty and affection, to bring him up as her nephew.

When Michael was six, he asked why he could not call Helen Mummy, as other boys called their mothers, and she gently explained that she was only his auntie. <break time="0.8s" /> Since he was so eager, however, she allowed him to use the word at bedtime as a private pet name, a secret to be shared only between the two of them. <break time="0.8s" /> Michael kept the secret faithfully, but when he discovered that Helen had told her friends about it, he flew into a furious rage that astonished her. <break time="0.8s" /> Why did you tell, he cried at the end of the storm, and he declared that he would never call her Mummy again, not even at bedtime. <break time="0.8s" /> At ten, after two terms at a preparatory school, Michael came to understand the truth about his birth, and he wondered anxiously whether Helen would think less of him. <break time="0.8s" /> Far from pushing him away, Helen reassured him so tenderly that the two of them grew closer than ever, and the subject was not raised again for years. <break time="0.8s" /> Later, when he lay delirious with measles at his public school, the old question returned in his fever, and once more Helen calmed and comforted him. <break time="0.8s" /> Michael grew into a clever young man, and in the summer of 1914 he was looking forward to going up to Oxford with a scholarship in October.

But when the war broke out that August, Michael, who had been a sergeant in his schools Officers Training Corps, wanted to enlist at once as an ordinary soldier. <break time="0.8s" /> Instead, he was persuaded to accept a commission in a battalion so new that some of its men still wore old red uniforms, and so he became a lieutenant. <break time="0.8s" /> For months the battalion guarded the English coast and a Scottish estuary, and not until later was it sent to France, where it moved from one sector to another before reaching Ypres. <break time="0.8s" /> Michael wrote home that there was nothing special going on, but about a month later a fragment of a shell, falling out of a wet dawn, killed him instantly. <break time="0.8s" /> The next shell buried his body beneath the ruined foundations of a barn wall, and for a long time no trace of him could be found. <break time="0.8s" /> When the telegram announced that Michael was missing, Helen told herself that missing always means dead, and the inquiries she made through various organizations brought her no news. <break time="0.8s" /> In the months that followed she felt strangely numb, as if life were going on somewhere far away, and even the Armistice, which ended the war, passed over her unnoticed. <break time="0.8s" /> At last she was officially informed that his body had been found, identified, and buried again in Hagenzeele Third Military Cemetery, and she received his identity disc and watch.
